title: OS-Omni: A Cross-Platform Benchmark for Generalist Computer-Using Agents
claim: A modular evaluation system turns declarative task specifications into agent runs and executable final-state checks across many platforms.
layout: 5 stacked boxed panels, left config beside right modules, arrows tracing control flow
description: A dense system architecture diagram of the benchmark infrastructure. The left column shows a task.yaml config for a GIMP grayscale task, with color-highlighted fields for task, init, evaluation, limits and metadata. The right column stacks four rounded panels. Specification merges execution.yaml and task.yaml into a Normalized TaskSpec. Agent Loop contains an Agent node and a chain: Screenshot Capture, Prompt Builder, LLM Client + Planner, Action Parser. Execution Control holds a coordinator, Spec Loader, Episode Runner, Platform Controller Interface, Set-up, Post-Process and evaluator context. A bottom Platform & Evaluation band lists Linux, Windows, macOS, Android and iOS, with evaluator layers feeding Reward and Artifacts outputs. Pastel colors match YAML fields to the modules that use them, and orange arrows trace control flow. The eye goes first to the YAML on the left, then to the module boxes.
caption: Overview of the OS-OMNI environment infrastructure. Execution specifications select tasks, models, observation modes, and action modes; platform runners instantiate the corresponding runtime, run the agent loop, and invoke task-specific evaluators. To study this setting, we introduce OS-OMNI, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and web environments. Rather than a fixed task pool, OS-OMNI is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks (v1, v2, ...), and each new version includes more mock applications and harder tasks (Section 3.3). This paper focuses on the first release, v1. Each task specifies a naturallanguage instruction, reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and an executable final-state evaluator. On v1, we evaluate nine models: GPT-6-Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 4 Argon, GLM-5.3-753B, Kimi K3, Qwen 3.8 Max, Qwen 3.8 27B, Qwen 3.8 9B, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. The strongest model, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, 8.8 points below the human reference of 77.3%. Performance is highly uneven across platforms: all three frontier models (GPT-6-Astra, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4) exceed the human success rate on Linux, yet the best iOS and macOS results (41.7% and 54.2%) remain 33.5 and 25.6 points
abstract: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-device workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 69.1% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.2 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes. Our code, environments, scripts, and data are available at a project page.
